nodes.label: Persian rule of Egypt
nodes.full: The Achaemenid Second Persian Period (343–332), which Alexander ended — Egypt's foreign administration and the resentment of it are the ground the Ptolemaic settlement is built on.
nodes.src: background — see the folio egypt-664bc-332bc (The Late Period)

nodes.label: The Seleucid Empire
nodes.full: The rival Hellenistic empire of Syria and the east, the Ptolemies' opponent through six Syrian Wars over Coele-Syria; Antiochus III took the province for good, and Antiochus IV nearly took Egypt.
nodes.src: background — added on review; John Grainger, The Syrian Wars (2010)

nodes.label: The Roman Republic
nodes.full: Rome moved from friend (273) to protector (200) to arbiter (168) to creditor (59) to conqueror (30), the external power whose shadow lengthens across the whole later part of the folio.
nodes.src: background — added on review; Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)

nodes.label: Roman Egypt
nodes.full: After 30 BC Egypt was the personal domain of the Roman emperor, governed by an equestrian prefect and closed to senators — the wealthiest single addition ever made to the Roman state.
nodes.src: background — added on review; belongs to the next folio; Bowman, Egypt after the Pharaohs (1986)

nodes.label: Alexander the Great takes Egypt
nodes.full: Alexander entered Egypt in the winter of 332 to no resistance, the Persian satrap Mazaces handing it over. He sacrificed to the Apis bull at Memphis, was crowned there in pharaonic style, marked out the new city of Alexandria on the coast, and trekked to the oracle of Amun at Siwa, which is said to have greeted him as the god's son. He left within months, appointing Egyptian nomarchs under a Greek financial overseer, and never returned; his body did.
nodes.src: Arrian, Anabasis 3.1–5; Diodorus 17.49–52; Curtius 4.7–8. Alexandria's foundation: P.M. Fraser, Ptolemaic Alexandria (1972) vol.1 pp.3–7. Stanley Burstein, 'Alexander in Egypt', in Bosworth & Baynham (eds.), Alexander the Great in Fact and Fiction (2000).

nodes.label: Philip Arrhidaeus and Alexander IV — the empty kingship
nodes.full: After Alexander's death Egypt was ruled in the name of his half-brother Philip Arrhidaeus and his posthumous son Alexander IV, but governed by the satrap Ptolemy, who intercepted Alexander's funeral cortège and installed the body at Memphis (later Alexandria) as a talisman of legitimacy. Both Argead kings were murdered in the succession wars — Arrhidaeus in 317, the boy Alexander IV around 309 — leaving Ptolemy free to take the crown himself.
nodes.src: Diodorus 18.3, 18.28 (the funeral carriage), 19.105 (Alexander IV's death). Pausanias 1.6.3. Hölbl, A History of the Ptolemaic Empire (2001) pp.14–20.

nodes.label: Ptolemy I Soter — the founder
nodes.full: Ptolemy son of Lagos, one of Alexander's marshals, turned the satrapy of Egypt into a hereditary Greek kingdom. He beat off Perdiccas's invasion in 321, fought the other Successors across Cyprus, Syria and the Aegean, and took the royal title in 305. He founded the state cult of Serapis, began the Museum and Library, wrote a sober history of Alexander's campaigns, and set the pattern the dynasty followed for three centuries — a Macedonian court at Alexandria over a bureaucratised Egyptian country.
nodes.src: Satrap Stela (Cairo CG 22182), 311 BC. Diodorus 18–20; Ptolemy's lost history underlies Arrian. Hölbl (2001) pp.21–35; Walter Ellis, Ptolemy of Egypt (1994).

nodes.label: Ptolemy II Philadelphus — the golden age
nodes.full: Under Ptolemy II the Museum and Library reached their height, the Pharos lighthouse was finished, and a spectacular procession through Alexandria advertised the dynasty's wealth to the Greek world. He married his full sister Arsinoe II, and the pair were worshipped as the 'Sibling Gods'. He re-cut the Nile–Red Sea canal, planted Greek soldier-settlers across a newly drained Faiyum, financed the Alexandrian poets, and fought the first two of the long Syrian Wars.
nodes.src: Grand Procession: Kallixeinos of Rhodes via Athenaeus 5.196–203; E.E. Rice, The Grand Procession of Ptolemy Philadelphus (1983). Faiyum: the Zenon archive. Hölbl (2001) pp.35–46, 61–63.

nodes.label: Ptolemy III Euergetes — the empire at its widest
nodes.full: In the Third Syrian War Ptolemy III marched east as far as Babylon and beyond, according to his own Adulis inscription, and brought home cult statues the Persians had carried off from Egypt centuries before — earning the title Euergetes, 'Benefactor'. His empire reached its greatest extent, taking in coastal strips from Thrace to Cyrenaica. He began the great temple of Horus at Edfu in 237 and issued the Canopus Decree, a priestly synod's attempt to fix the drifting calendar with a leap day.
nodes.src: Adulis inscription: OGIS 54; Cosmas Indicopleustes preserves it. Canopus Decree (Cairo CG 22186 and the Tanis and Kom el-Hisn copies), 238 BC. Edfu foundation: the temple's own building texts. Hölbl (2001) pp.46–52.

nodes.label: Ptolemy IV Philopator — Raphia and the turn
nodes.full: Ptolemy IV won the Fourth Syrian War at Raphia in 217, but only by arming and training some 20,000 native Egyptians as a phalanx — a decision Polybius blamed for the revolts that followed, since the men who had won the battle would not go back to being subjects. His court was run by the ministers Sosibius and Agathocles, who had his mother and brother killed; the king is drawn in the sources as an indolent aesthete, and his death in 204 was concealed while the ministers seized power.
nodes.src: Polybius 5.34–87 (Raphia and its consequences). Raphia Decree (trilingual; Cairo and Pithom copies), 217 BC. The palace coup on his death: Polybius 15.25–33. Hölbl (2001) pp.127–33.

nodes.label: Ptolemy V Epiphanes — the Rosetta king
nodes.full: Ptolemy V came to the throne as a small child amid palace murders, a Delta revolt, and the ongoing secession of the Thebaid. Antiochus III seized Coele-Syria at the Battle of Panium in 200, and Rome stepped in as the boy-king's protector. His formal coronation at Memphis in 196 was marked by a priestly decree of thanks, cut in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek on the stone found at Rosetta in 1799 that unlocked the Egyptian scripts.
nodes.src: Rosetta Stone / Memphis Decree (BM EA 24), 196 BC. Polybius 18.53–54; Livy 33.19–20. Hölbl (2001) pp.134–43, 153–59; Richard Parkinson, The Rosetta Stone (2005).

nodes.label: Ptolemy VI Philometor — the reign of civil war and Rome
nodes.full: Ptolemy VI spent his reign at odds with his brother Ptolemy VIII, the two dividing and re-dividing the kingdom. When Antiochus IV invaded in 170 and 168 and stood outside Alexandria, only a Roman ultimatum — the envoy Popillius Laenas drawing a line in the sand — made him withdraw. Cyrenaica was split off for Ptolemy VIII by Roman arrangement. Philometor was, by the standards of the late dynasty, a capable king; he died of a fall from his horse campaigning in Syria.
nodes.src: Polybius 28–29; Diodorus 31.1–2. The partition of the kingdom and Cyrene: the 'Testament of Ptolemy VIII' (SEG 9.7). Hölbl (2001) pp.143–52, 181–94.

nodes.label: Ptolemy VIII Euergetes II 'Physcon'
nodes.full: Ptolemy VIII returned from Cyrene on his brother's death to rule Egypt, marrying first his sister Cleopatra II and then, alongside her, his niece Cleopatra III. His war with Cleopatra II from 132 tore the country apart for a decade, ending in the amnesty decrees of 118. His purges of the Alexandrian Greek elite, remembered by Menecles of Barca, scattered scholars and artists across the Mediterranean and are often said to have ended Alexandria's cultural pre-eminence.
nodes.src: The 118 BC amnesty decrees: P. Tebtunis I 5. Menecles of Barca on the intellectual exodus: FGrH 270 F 9 via Athenaeus 4.184b–c. Hölbl (2001) pp.194–203.

nodes.label: The later Ptolemies — dynasty at war with itself
nodes.full: After Physcon the dynasty consumed itself in wars between Cleopatra III and her sons Ptolemy IX and Ptolemy X, and between the brothers. A revolt in the Thebaid was crushed in 88 with the sacking of Thebes, which never recovered. Rome inherited Cyrenaica in 96 and increasingly treated Egypt as a bequest waiting to be collected, its intervention held off only by the value of the grain and the size of the bribes.
nodes.src: Pausanias 1.9; Justin 39. The 88 BC Theban revolt and sack: Pausanias 1.9.3. The 'will' bequeathing Egypt to Rome (Ptolemy X or XI): Cicero, De Rege Alexandrino. Hölbl (2001) pp.204–13.

nodes.label: Ptolemy XII Auletes — the client king
nodes.full: Ptolemy XII bought Roman recognition of his rule in 59 BC with a bribe to Caesar and Pompey said to be 6,000 talents, borrowed from the financier Rabirius. He could not prevent Rome annexing Cyprus in 58, was driven out by an Alexandrian mob, and was put back on his throne in 55 by the Syrian governor Gabinius, who left a garrison of Roman soldiers behind. He died in 51 having pledged Egypt's revenues to his Roman creditors and named his daughter Cleopatra and a son as joint heirs.
nodes.src: Cicero, letters and Pro Rabirio Postumo; Dio Cassius 39.12–16, 39.55–58. Hölbl (2001) pp.222–30; Mary Siani-Davies, 'Ptolemy XII Auletes and the Romans', Historia 46 (1997).

nodes.label: Cleopatra VII Philopator
nodes.full: Cleopatra VII ruled first with her brother Ptolemy XIII, who drove her out; Julius Caesar, arriving in 48, restored her, fought the Alexandrian War for her, and fathered her son Caesarion. After Caesar's murder she backed and then married Mark Antony, bore him three children, and received from him at the Donations of Alexandria in 34 grants of Roman eastern territory for her children. Octavian's propaganda made her Rome's enemy; defeat at Actium in 31 and his invasion in 30 ended the dynasty, and she took her own life.
nodes.src: Plutarch, Antony; Dio Cassius 42–51; Caesar, Bellum Alexandrinum. Duane Roller, Cleopatra: A Biography (2010); Joyce Tyldesley, Cleopatra: Last Queen of Egypt (2008).

nodes.label: Caesarion — the last king
nodes.full: Ptolemy XV Caesar, called Caesarion, was Cleopatra's son by Julius Caesar and her co-ruler from the age of three, styled 'King of Kings' at the Donations of Alexandria. After Actium his mother sent him toward the Red Sea and India for safety, but he was lured back and killed on Octavian's orders — reportedly on the advice 'it is not good to have too many Caesars'. With him the three-thousand-year line of Egyptian kingship ended.
nodes.src: Plutarch, Antony 81–82; Suetonius, Augustus 17; Dio Cassius 51.15. The 'too many Caesars' line attributed to the philosopher Arius via Plutarch.

nodes.label: Horwennefer and Ankhwennefer — the rebel kings of Thebes
nodes.full: During the Great Revolt of the Thebaid, Upper Egypt seceded under two successive native kings, Horwennefer and then Ankhwennefer, who took full pharaonic titles, dated documents by their own regnal years, were recognised by the Theban temples, and drew support from the Kingdom of Meroe to the south. They held Thebes and much of the south for the better part of twenty years before a Ptolemaic army under Komanos defeated Ankhwennefer in 186; an amnesty decree formally closed the war.
nodes.src: Demotic and Greek documents dated by their reigns; the Philae priestly decree of 186 recording the victory. Anne-Emmanuelle Veïsse, Les 'révoltes égyptiennes': Recherches sur les troubles intérieurs en Égypte du règne de Ptolémée III à la conquête romaine (2004); Hölbl (2001) pp.153–59.

nodes.label: Harsiese — a native king in the dynastic war
nodes.full: While Ptolemy VIII and Cleopatra II fought their civil war, a man named Harsiese was briefly proclaimed king at Thebes, issuing at least one order to a bank and appearing in a handful of Demotic documents before vanishing from the record. His short-lived kingship shows that native royal claims in the south could still resurface whenever the dynasty's grip slipped.
nodes.src: P. Amherst 51 and related Demotic texts; Pieter Pestman, 'Haronnophris and Chaonnophris', in Vleeming (ed.), Hundred-Gated Thebes (1995); Veïsse, Les 'révoltes égyptiennes' (2004).

nodes.label: The ruling Cleopatras
nodes.full: Long before Cleopatra VII, the dynasty gave real power to its queens. Cleopatra I, a Seleucid princess, ruled as regent for her son Ptolemy V and issued coinage and decrees in her own name. Cleopatra II was co-ruler, then led an armed revolt against her brother-husband Ptolemy VIII and held Alexandria for years. Cleopatra III wielded decisive influence over her sons' reigns. The pattern of the queen as an independent centre of power was a Ptolemaic institution.
nodes.src: Cleopatra I's regency: Polybius 22.3; coins and dating formulae. Cleopatra II's revolt: the 132–124 BC documents. Grace Macurdy, Hellenistic Queens (1932); Elizabeth Carney, Arsinoë of Egypt and Macedon (2013) for the wider pattern.

nodes.label: Alexander takes Egypt
nodes.full: Alexander's army crossed Sinai and reached Pelusium in the autumn of 332; the Persian satrap Mazaces, left without troops after Issus and the fall of the Levant, surrendered the country. There was no battle. Alexander sailed up the Nile to Memphis, was received as a liberator from Persian rule, held games and sacrifices, and turned the moment into a change of dynasty rather than a conquest.
nodes.src: Arrian, Anabasis 3.1; Curtius 4.7.1–5. Stanley Burstein, 'Alexander in Egypt: Continuity or Change?', in Achaemenid History 8 (1994).

nodes.label: Ptolemy secures Egypt
nodes.full: Ptolemy fought off the other marshals to keep Egypt. In 321 the regent Perdiccas invaded and lost thousands of men trying to force the Nile at Memphis, drowned or taken by crocodiles, and was killed by his own officers. Ptolemy then contested Cyprus, Cyrene and Coele-Syria for two decades, winning the Battle of Gaza in 312 and losing ground again, until the coalition victory over Antigonus at Ipsus in 301 left him securely holding Egypt and southern Syria.
nodes.src: Diodorus 18.33–36 (Perdiccas at the Nile), 19.80–86 (Gaza), 20.113, 21.1 (Ipsus). Hölbl, A History of the Ptolemaic Empire (2001) pp.14–24; Richard Billows, Antigonos the One-Eyed (1990).

nodes.label: The Syrian Wars
nodes.full: For over a century the Ptolemies and the Seleucids fought six wars, chiefly over Coele-Syria — the southern Levant, its ports, timber and taxes. Ptolemaic power crested in the Third War, when Ptolemy III overran Seleucid territory to the Euphrates; it broke in the Fifth, when Antiochus III took the province for good. The wars drained both kingdoms and drew in Rome, which ended the last of them with the ultimatum of 168.
nodes.src: Polybius 5, 15, 28–29; the Gurob Papyrus (Third War). Overview: John Grainger, The Syrian Wars (2010); Hölbl (2001) pp.38–52, 134–43.

nodes.label: The Battle of Raphia
nodes.full: At Raphia on the Gaza coast Ptolemy IV met Antiochus III with about 70,000 men and 73 African elephants against 68,000 and 102 Indian elephants. Antiochus' elephants and right wing broke through, but Ptolemy's centre — including 20,000 Egyptians newly trained in the Macedonian phalanx — held and won the day. Egypt kept Coele-Syria for another seventeen years, and a trilingual decree celebrated the victory; but the armed and confident native soldiery was a new political fact.
nodes.src: Polybius 5.79–87. Raphia Decree, 217 BC (Pithom and Memphis copies). Bezalel Bar-Kochva, The Seleucid Army (1976) pp.128–41.

nodes.label: The Great Revolt of the Thebaid
nodes.full: Beginning in the confusion after Ptolemy IV's death, Upper Egypt seceded under native pharaohs at Thebes and stayed out of Ptolemaic control for twenty years, funded partly by the temples and aided from Meroe. A separate rising in the Delta was crushed by Ptolemy V at Lycopolis, and the amnesty of 197 brought a brief peace. The Thebaid was only reconquered in 186; the temples of the south paid for their support with new controls and levies.
nodes.src: Polybius 22.17; the Rosetta and Philae decrees. Anne-Emmanuelle Veïsse, Les 'révoltes égyptiennes' (2004); Brian McGing, 'Revolt Egyptian Style', Archiv für Papyrusforschung 43 (1997).

nodes.label: The Battle of Panium and the loss of the empire
nodes.full: At Panium, near the sources of the Jordan, Antiochus III destroyed the Ptolemaic field army under Scopas. Coele-Syria, held since Ptolemy I, passed permanently to the Seleucids. It was the effective end of the Ptolemaic overseas empire: within a generation Cyprus and Cyrene were all that remained abroad, and the kingdom shrank back to the Nile valley, dependent on Rome to guarantee even that.
nodes.src: Polybius 16.18–19, 28.1; the 'Battle of Panium' fragment. Hölbl (2001) pp.134–39; Grainger, The Syrian Wars (2010) pp.245–58.

nodes.label: The Day of Eleusis
nodes.full: Antiochus IV, master of Egypt after two invasions and camped in the suburbs of Alexandria, was met by the Roman envoy Gaius Popillius Laenas carrying the Senate's decree that he leave Egypt. When Antiochus asked for time to consult his advisers, Popillius drew a circle in the sand around him with his staff and told him to answer before stepping out of it. Antiochus withdrew. Rome had settled the fate of the Hellenistic east without fighting.
nodes.src: Polybius 29.27; Livy 45.12; Diodorus 31.2. The episode's date is 30 June 168 BC (a lunar eclipse fixes it). Erich Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984).

nodes.label: The dynasty at war with itself
nodes.full: From Ptolemy VI on, the Ptolemies fought each other more than any foreign enemy: brother against brother, mother against son, the mob of Alexandria against whichever king it disliked, the chora against the capital. Cleopatra II held Alexandria in arms against Ptolemy VIII for a decade; a Theban revolt was put down in 88 with the sacking of the ancient city. Each round of civil war spent revenue, wrecked administration, and made Roman arbitration harder to refuse.
nodes.src: Polybius 31, 39; Diodorus 33–34; Justin 38–39. The sack of Thebes: Pausanias 1.9.3. Hölbl (2001) pp.181–213.

nodes.label: Actium and the annexation of Egypt
nodes.full: Antony and Cleopatra's fleet was beaten off Actium in western Greece in September 31, and their forces melted away over the following year. Octavian invaded Egypt from Syria in the summer of 30, took Pelusium and then Alexandria; Antony and then Cleopatra killed themselves, and Caesarion was hunted down and executed. Octavian annexed Egypt as his personal possession, governed by a prefect of equestrian rank and closed to senators — the wealthiest single addition ever made to the Roman state.
nodes.src: Plutarch, Antony 60–86; Dio Cassius 50–51; Suetonius, Augustus 17. The settlement: P.A. Brunt & J.M. Moore, Res Gestae Divi Augusti (1967); Alan Bowman, Egypt after the Pharaohs (1986) pp.37–44.

nodes.label: A Greek kingdom over an Egyptian country
nodes.full: The Ptolemaic state ran on a double footing. A Macedonian-Greek ruling class governed from Alexandria, and three Greek cities — Alexandria, Ptolemais in the south, and old Naukratis — kept Greek civic institutions. The rest of the country, the chora, was administered by adapted pharaonic methods in Greek and Demotic. Greek and Egyptian law both had force; the king was basileus to the Greeks and Pharaoh to the Egyptians, and largely kept the two worlds in separate documents.
nodes.src: Naphtali Lewis, Greeks in Ptolemaic Egypt (1986); Alan K. Bowman, Egypt after the Pharaohs (1986) pp.21–36. The legal duality: Joseph Mélèze Modrzejewski, 'Law and Justice in Ptolemaic Egypt', in Geller & Maehler (eds.), Legal Documents of the Hellenistic World (1995).

nodes.label: The dioiketes and the fiscal machine
nodes.full: Ptolemy II built the most systematically extractive government the ancient world had seen, run by a chief finance minister, the dioiketes. Every nome had a royal scribe keeping a fresh land-and-crop survey, an economic officer, and a military governor; taxes on land, orchards, salt, beer, oil and dozens of trades were farmed out to bidders backed by sureties; and a set of Revenue Laws laid down the procedure. The minister Apollonios and his agent Zenon left an archive of over 1,700 documents showing it at work.
nodes.src: Revenue Laws Papyrus (P. Rev.), 259 BC: Bingen, Le papyrus Revenue Laws (1952). Zenon archive: Pieter Pestman, A Guide to the Zenon Archive (1981). Sitta von Reden, Money in Ptolemaic Egypt (2007).

nodes.label: The cleruchy
nodes.full: The Ptolemies settled their soldiers on the land. A cleruch received a plot of royal ground — larger for cavalry, smaller for infantry — held rent-light in return for turning out when summoned, and increasingly passed to his sons. The policy planted tens of thousands of Greek, Thracian, Jewish and other military families across the countryside, above all in the reclaimed Faiyum, creating a Hellenised rural elite alongside the Egyptian peasantry and, at Raphia, extending to armed Egyptians too.
nodes.src: Jane Rowlandson (ed.), Women and Society in Greek and Roman Egypt (1998) on cleruchic families; Christelle Fischer-Bovet, Army and Society in Ptolemaic Egypt (2014). The Faiyum toponymy (Philadelphia, Theadelphia, etc.) records the settlement.

nodes.label: The bilingual archive
nodes.full: Ptolemaic government generated paper on an unprecedented scale, and Egypt's dry sand kept it. Greek was the language of the higher administration; Demotic served private Egyptian law and the temples; official notaries of both kinds registered contracts. The surviving papyri — the Zenon, Tebtunis, Herakleopolis and other archives, and later the vast Oxyrhynchus rubbish mounds — make Ptolemaic and Roman Egypt the best-documented pre-modern society anywhere.
nodes.src: Roger Bagnall, Reading Papyri, Writing Ancient History (1995); E.G. Turner, Greek Papyri: An Introduction (1968). Tebtunis: Grenfell, Hunt & Smyly, The Tebtunis Papyri (1902– ).

nodes.label: The priestly synods and the trilingual decrees
nodes.full: The high priests of Egypt's temples met in assembly, at first yearly, to conduct business with the crown: confirming honours for the king, setting festival calendars, and negotiating the temples' privileges and obligations. Their honorific decrees — issued at Canopus in 238, at Memphis for Ptolemy IV in 217 and for Ptolemy V in 196 — were published in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek, and are the formal record of the bargain between the Greek monarchy and the Egyptian religious establishment.
nodes.src: Canopus Decree (Cairo CG 22186); Raphia Decree; Memphis Decree / Rosetta Stone (BM EA 24). Stefan Pfeiffer, Das Dekret von Kanopos (2004); Christophe Thiers on the synodal decree corpus.

nodes.label: Greek courts, Egyptian courts, and the petition
nodes.full: Justice ran on parallel tracks: royal circuit judges (chrematistai) applied Greek law, Egyptian judges (laokritai) applied Egyptian law, and litigants could sometimes choose. Above both, any subject could send a written petition (enteuxis) to the king — in practice to an official acting in his name — and thousands survive, from stolen donkeys to violent assault to fraud by a tax-farmer. A decree of 118 BC set rules for which court heard cases between Greeks and Egyptians.
nodes.src: P. Tebtunis I 5 (the 118 BC decree). Petitions: John Bauschatz, Law and Enforcement in Ptolemaic Egypt (2013); the enteuxeis of P. Enteuxeis (O. Guéraud, 1931). Modrzejewski, The Laws of Moses and the Laws of Egypt.

nodes.label: Rome the overlord
nodes.full: Rome's grip tightened by stages. From 200 it was the boy Ptolemy V's protector; in 168 its envoy turned Antiochus IV out of Egypt with a word; in 59 Ptolemy XII bought recognition of his throne with a colossal bribe raised from Roman lenders; in 55 a Roman army restored him and left a garrison. By the time Cleopatra VII took the throne the kingdom's revenues were pledged to Roman financiers and its independence was a formality Rome could revoke at will.
nodes.src: Polybius; Cicero, Pro Rabirio Postumo and letters. Erich Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984) vol.2; Mary Siani-Davies, Cicero's Speech Pro Rabirio Postumo (2001).

nodes.label: Serapis and the cult of the living king
nodes.full: Ptolemy I promoted Serapis — the Memphite Osiris-Apis reshaped with a Greek-god's face and body — as a deity both Greeks and Egyptians could worship, and built him a great temple on the Alexandrian acropolis. The dynasty also had itself worshipped: living Ptolemies and their queens received divine cult, an eponymous priest of Alexander and the deified rulers headed the state calendar, and Arsinoe II after her death was given her own priestess and a share in every temple in the land.
nodes.src: John E. Stambaugh, Sarapis under the Early Ptolemies (1972). Ruler cult: Ludwig Koenen, 'The Ptolemaic King as a Religious Figure', in Bulloch et al. (eds.), Images and Ideologies (1993). Arsinoe: the Mendes Stela; Elizabeth Carney, Arsinoë of Egypt and Macedon (2013).

nodes.label: The Egyptian temple rebuilt at its grandest
nodes.full: The Ptolemies, for all their Greekness, poured resources into Egyptian temples, and the best-preserved of all Egyptian temples are theirs. The temple of Horus at Edfu, begun in 237 and finished 180 years later, stands almost complete, its walls a library of ritual, myth and temple lore in dense Ptolemaic hieroglyphs. Dendera, Kom Ombo, Esna, Philae and the birth-houses belong to the same programme — the classic Egyptian sanctuary in its final, most elaborate form.
nodes.src: Dieter Arnold, Temples of the Last Pharaohs (1999) pp.137–224. Edfu texts: the Chassinat/Rochemonteix edition, Le temple d'Edfou (1892– ); Sylvie Cauville's studies. Philae: the pre-flood documentation.

nodes.label: The meeting of Greek and Egyptian gods
nodes.full: Three centuries of coexistence blended the two religious worlds. Isis grew from an Egyptian goddess into a Mediterranean-wide saviour, her powers catalogued in Greek 'aretalogies' that begin 'I am Isis'; Thoth was read as Hermes Trismegistos; the child Horus became Harpocrates. Greeks in Egypt worshipped Egyptian gods under Greek names and Egyptian priests wrote their theology in Greek forms, while the temples of the chora carried on in pure Egyptian idiom.
nodes.src: Isis aretalogies: the Kyme, Maroneia and Andros texts; Jan Bergman, Ich bin Isis (1968). Françoise Dunand, Le culte d'Isis dans le bassin oriental de la Méditerranée (1973). David Frankfurter, Religion in Roman Egypt (1998) for the later trajectory.

nodes.label: The animal cults under royal patronage
nodes.full: The Ptolemies funded and joined Egypt's animal cults. Kings attended the enthronement and burial of the Apis at Memphis and the Buchis bull at Armant, whose gallery cemetery, the Bucheum, and the associated Mothers-of-Buchis cemetery date largely to this period. The ibis, falcon, cat and crocodile necropoleis stayed busy, and the votive-mummy industry — a prayer carried to a god by a purpose-mummified animal — reached its greatest scale.
nodes.src: Robert Mond & Oliver Myers, The Bucheum, 3 vols. (1934). Dorothy Thompson, Memphis under the Ptolemies (1988, 2nd ed. 2012) on the Apis. Salima Ikram (ed.), Divine Creatures (2005).

nodes.label: The Jews of Egypt and the temple of Onias
nodes.full: Egypt held the largest Jewish community outside Judaea — two of Alexandria's five districts, and settlements across the chora, many descended from soldiers. Their synagogues (proseuchai) carried dedications 'on behalf of King Ptolemy'. Around 160 BC the exiled Zadokite high priest Onias IV was allowed to build a functioning Jewish temple at Leontopolis, which operated for over two centuries — the tradition within which the Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures, the Septuagint, took shape.
nodes.src: Josephus, Antiquities 12–13, Jewish War 7.10.2–4 (Onias' temple); the Letter of Aristeas (Septuagint legend). Corpus Papyrorum Judaicarum (Tcherikover & Fuks, 1957–64); Sylvie Honigman, The Septuagint and Homeric Scholarship in Alexandria (2003).

nodes.label: The Oracle of the Potter and apocalyptic
nodes.full: A strand of Demotic literature turned religion against the Greeks. The Oracle of the Potter, surviving in Greek translations from Egyptian, prophesies that the 'city by the sea' — Alexandria — will be emptied and become a place where fishermen dry their nets, its founding god departing to Memphis, and that a saviour king 'sent by the Sun' will restore Egypt and its temples. The Demotic Chronicle reads the succession of kings for the same promise of deliverance from foreign rule.
nodes.src: Oracle of the Potter: Ludwig Koenen, Die Prophezeiungen des Toepfers, ZPE 2 (1968) and later. Demotic Chronicle: P. BN 215. David Frankfurter, Elijah in Upper Egypt (1993) pp.159–94 on the apocalyptic tradition.

nodes.label: Alexandrian poetry
nodes.full: The court and Library at Alexandria produced a new kind of Greek poetry — learned, polished, allusive, short. Callimachus wrote the Aetia and the hymns and declared that 'a big book is a big evil'; Theocritus invented the pastoral idyll and set one poem among Alexandrian housewives at a festival; Apollonius of Rhodes wrote the epic Argonautica; Herodas the sharp little verse mimes. Their aesthetic of erudite miniaturism defined 'Hellenistic' literature and, through Rome, shaped Catullus and the Augustan poets.
nodes.src: Callimachus: Pfeiffer's edition (1949–53). Theocritus, Idyll 15 (the Adoniazusae). Apollonius: R.L. Hunter's commentary. Overview: Kathryn Gutzwiller, A Guide to Hellenistic Literature (2007).

nodes.label: The temple as a written world
nodes.full: The Ptolemaic temple was a text as much as a building. Every surface at Edfu and Dendera carries inscription — cosmology, the daily ritual, the local mythology, the temple's own foundation legend, festival calendars, drama scripts such as the Edfu 'Triumph of Horus', pharmacological and geographical lists. The astronomical ceilings, including the circular zodiac from Dendera, map the sky. The temple presented itself as a model of the ordered universe, and much of what we know of late Egyptian religion is copied from these walls.
nodes.src: Edfu: Chassinat, Le temple d'Edfou (1892– ); Dieter Kurth, Edfou (translations). Dendera zodiac (now Louvre): Sylvie Cauville, Le zodiaque d'Osiris (1997). The Triumph of Horus: H.W. Fairman (1974).

nodes.label: Greco-Egyptian art
nodes.full: Ptolemaic art spoke two visual languages at once. The same king appears on a coin as a Greek Hellenistic ruler and on a temple wall as a traditional pharaoh; a limestone stela can carry Greek-style modelling above Egyptian-style registers. Sculptors developed a distinct 'Ptolemaic' portrait — smooth, round-faced, with the archaising back-pillar — and workshops turned out faience wine-jugs stamped with a queen pouring a libation and thousands of terracotta figurines mixing Bes, Isis and Greek genre types.
nodes.src: Robert Bianchi (ed.), Cleopatra's Egypt: Age of the Ptolemies (1988). Faience oinochoai: Dorothy Burr Thompson, Ptolemaic Oinochoai and Portraits in Faience (1973). Paul Stanwick, Portraits of the Ptolemies (2002).

nodes.label: Alexandria, the model Hellenistic city
nodes.full: Laid out on a grid between the sea and Lake Mareotis, with a broad colonnaded main street and a made harbour, Alexandria became the template for the Hellenistic capital. Its royal quarter held the palaces, the Museum and Library, the theatre, and the Sema, the tomb where Alexander's body lay in state. A kilometre-long causeway, the Heptastadion, joined the city to the island of Pharos and split the harbour in two. Within a century it was the largest city in the Greek world.
nodes.src: Strabo 17.1.6–10. P.M. Fraser, Ptolemaic Alexandria (1972); Judith McKenzie, The Architecture of Alexandria and Egypt (2007). The submerged royal quarter: Franck Goddio's Portus Magnus survey.

nodes.label: Demotic literature
nodes.full: Egyptian storytelling flourished in its own script and language. The Setne Khamwas cycle follows a magician-prince who steals a book of Thoth and pays for it; the 'Myth of the Sun's Eye' frames a cycle of animal fables as a philosophical dialogue between a small cat-goddess and a baboon; and the Tebtunis temple library, excavated intact, held wisdom texts, ritual, astrology, dream-books and narrative in Demotic and hieratic. It is a parallel literary culture to the Greek one at Alexandria, largely invisible to it.
nodes.src: Setne I and II: F.Ll. Griffith, Stories of the High Priests of Memphis (1900). Myth of the Sun's Eye: Wilhelm Spiegelberg (1917); the Lille Demotic version. Tebtunis library: Kim Ryholt, The Carlsberg Papyri (2005– ).

nodes.label: The theatre, the guild and the water-organ
nodes.full: Alexandria had a full Greek performance culture: a theatre in the palace quarter, the great Ptolemaia festival with its games, and a resident branch of the 'Artists of Dionysus', the international guild of actors, musicians and poets who toured the Hellenistic world with royal privileges. It was here that the engineer Ktesibios built the first keyboard instrument, the hydraulis or water-organ, using air pressure regulated by a water column — an invention that spread across the Roman world.
nodes.src: Technitai of Dionysus: Brigitte Le Guen, Les associations de technites dionysiaques (2001). Hydraulis: Vitruvius 10.8; Athenaeus 4.174; surviving fragments from Dion and Aquincum. Ktesibios: Drachmann, The Mechanical Technology of Greek and Roman Antiquity (1963).

nodes.label: The painted shroud and the bicultural dead
nodes.full: Ptolemaic elite burial worked out a visual compromise. Bodies were still mummified and equipped for an Egyptian afterlife, but the coverings changed: painted linen shrouds and cartonnage masks began to combine Egyptian protective imagery with faces rendered in an increasingly Greek, naturalistic style, sometimes framed by Egyptian gods. The Faiyum cemeteries where this develops are the same ones that, under Rome, produced the famous encaustic mummy portraits.
nodes.src: Christina Riggs, The Beautiful Burial in Roman Egypt (2005) traces the Ptolemaic roots. Hawara: Petrie, Hawara, Biahmu and Arsinoe (1889) and Roman Portraits and Memphis IV (1911).

nodes.label: The Museum and the Library
nodes.full: The Ptolemies founded, next to the palace, a 'shrine of the Muses' — a state-funded research community whose members drew royal salaries, ate at a common table, and worked in a complex with covered walks, lecture rooms and the Library. Agents bought or copied books across the Greek world, sometimes keeping the originals; ancient estimates of the collection run from tens of thousands to half a million rolls. It was the first institution to make scholarship a salaried, collective, permanent activity.
nodes.src: Strabo 17.1.8; the Letter of Aristeas; Galen on the 'ship's books'. P.M. Fraser, Ptolemaic Alexandria (1972) vol.1 pp.305–35; Roy MacLeod (ed.), The Library of Alexandria (2000).

nodes.label: Euclid and the axiomatic method
nodes.full: Euclid, working at Alexandria around 300, compiled the Elements: thirteen books deriving the whole of the era's geometry and number theory from a short list of definitions, postulates and common notions by explicit proof. It became the most influential textbook ever written and the model for what a rigorous argument looks like. Alexandria stayed the centre of Greek mathematics for centuries — Apollonius of Perga's Conics, on the ellipse, parabola and hyperbola, was written in the same tradition.
nodes.src: Euclid, Elements: Heiberg's text; Thomas Heath's translation and commentary (1908). Apollonius, Conics: books 1–4 in Greek, 5–7 via Arabic. Reviel Netz, The Shaping of Deduction in Greek Mathematics (1999).

nodes.label: Eratosthenes measures the Earth
nodes.full: Eratosthenes of Cyrene, chief Librarian under Ptolemy III, calculated the circumference of the Earth from the difference in the sun's noon shadow between Syene, where at the solstice it cast none, and Alexandria — arriving at a figure within a few per cent of the true value. He also drew a world map on a grid of parallels and meridians, estimated the tilt of the Earth's axis, and produced a scholarly chronology of Greek history. Contemporaries nicknamed him 'Beta', second-best at everything.
nodes.src: Cleomedes, On the Heavens 1.7 preserves the measurement. Duane Roller, Eratosthenes' Geography (2010). The 'Beta' nickname: Suda s.v. Eratosthenes.

nodes.label: Herophilus, Erasistratus and human anatomy
nodes.full: For a few decades under the first Ptolemies, dissection of human bodies — and, the Roman writer Celsus alleged, vivisection of condemned prisoners — was permitted at Alexandria and nowhere else. Herophilus described the nervous system, distinguished sensory from motor nerves, named parts of the brain and eye, and studied the pulse; Erasistratus traced the heart valves and the branching of veins and arteries. Ancient anatomy reached a level not matched again until the Renaissance, then the licence closed.
nodes.src: Celsus, De Medicina, proem 23–26. Heinrich von Staden, Herophilus: The Art of Medicine in Early Alexandria (1989); James Longrigg, Greek Rational Medicine (1993).

nodes.label: The moving Earth and the mechanised sky
nodes.full: Aristarchus of Samos, who worked at Alexandria, proposed that the Earth turns on its axis and orbits a central Sun, and tried to measure the relative distances of Sun and Moon — a hypothesis the mainstream rejected but did not forget. The court astronomer Conon claimed a new constellation, the 'Lock of Berenice', from a queen's dedicated hair. The same Alexandrian and Rhodian milieu built geared calendar-and-planet computers of the kind later found in the Antikythera wreck.
nodes.src: Aristarchus: Archimedes, Sand-Reckoner 1.4–5; Thomas Heath, Aristarchus of Samos (1913). Lock of Berenice: Callimachus, Aetia fr.110; Catullus 66. Antikythera mechanism: Freeth et al., Nature 444 (2006) and 454 (2008).

nodes.label: Exploring the Red Sea and Africa
nodes.full: Egypt was the Hellenistic world's window on the Indian Ocean and inner Africa. Ptolemaic elephant-hunting expeditions along the African coast produced the first Greek surveys of it; a court official, Agatharchides of Cnidus, wrote On the Erythraean Sea describing the peoples, the gold-mining, and the navigation of the Red Sea; and the geographers of the Museum folded these reports into the first attempts at a scientific map of the whole known world.
nodes.src: Agatharchides, On the Erythraean Sea: Stanley Burstein's translation and commentary (1989). Elephant stations: Strabo 16.4; the Pithom Stela. Lionel Casson, The Periplus Maris Erythraei (1989) for the (later) sequel.

nodes.label: Egyptian temple learning and Manetho
nodes.full: Alongside the Greek Museum, the Egyptian temples kept their own scholarship in the House of Life — ritual, astronomy, medicine, magic, the sacred scripts — passed down by hereditary priests and, at Tebtunis, preserved as an actual library. From this world the priest Manetho of Sebennytos wrote, in Greek and for the Greek kings, an Aegyptiaca: a history of Egypt divided into the thirty dynasties still used today. The two knowledge systems worked in parallel, translating each other only occasionally.
nodes.src: Manetho: Waddell's Loeb (1940); Gerald Verbrugghe & John Wickersham, Berossos and Manetho (1996). The temple libraries: Kim Ryholt & Gojko Barjamovic (eds.), Libraries before Alexandria (2019).

nodes.label: The royal monopoly economy
nodes.full: The Ptolemaic crown ran the most tightly managed economy of antiquity. Most farmland was royal land, worked by tenant 'royal farmers' to state quotas; the production and sale of vegetable oil, textiles, salt, papyrus, beer, honey and mine metals were state monopolies, contracted out under detailed rules; and a network of royal banks handled the money. The 259 BC Revenue Laws papyrus lays out the oil monopoly clause by clause — fixed prices, licensed presses, sealed stores, informers.
nodes.src: Revenue Laws Papyrus: Bingen (1952). M. Rostovtzeff, The Social and Economic History of the Hellenistic World (1941) vol.1; J.G. Manning, The Last Pharaohs: Egypt under the Ptolemies (2010); Sitta von Reden, Money in Ptolemaic Egypt (2007).

nodes.label: The reclaimed Faiyum
nodes.full: Ptolemy II lowered Lake Moeris again and drained its margins, adding perhaps 1,200 square kilometres of farmland, and settled it with Greek and other soldier-colonists in new villages with Greek names — Philadelphia, Theadelphia, Euhemeria. The dioiketes Apollonios ran a 10,000-aroura model estate at Philadelphia, and his agent Zenon's papers record the experiments: imported hard wheat, Milesian sheep, new vines and fruit trees, and constant friction with the local labour.
nodes.src: Zenon archive: P.Cair.Zen., P.Lond. VII, P.Mich. I; Pieter Pestman, A Guide to the Zenon Archive (1981). Faiyum reclamation: Katja Mueller, Settlements of the Ptolemies (2006); Dorothy Thompson in Cambridge Ancient History VII.1 (1984).

nodes.label: Grain and the fleet
nodes.full: Egyptian grain fed the Hellenistic world. The state bought the harvest at fixed prices, stored it in Alexandria, and sold the surplus into the Aegean market or gave it away as diplomacy — grain aid to Rhodes after its earthquake, to Athens, to Rome in a famine. Alexandria's twin harbours and the ships that used them made the city the pivot of the eastern Mediterranean food supply, a role it kept for another seven centuries under Rome and Byzantium.
nodes.src: Grain diplomacy: the Rhodian earthquake, Polybius 5.88–90; the Athenian and Roman famine reliefs. Peter Garnsey, Famine and Food Supply in the Graeco-Roman World (1988); Alan Bowman & Andrew Wilson (eds.), The Roman Agricultural Economy (2013) for method.

nodes.label: The closed currency and the banks
nodes.full: The Ptolemies struck coin on a standard lighter than the Greek norm and ran a 'closed' currency zone: foreign coin had to be exchanged for Ptolemaic money at the frontier, keeping the difference for the crown. Heavy bronze coinage put money into everyday village transactions for the first time, monetising the Egyptian countryside. Royal and private banks took deposits, made loans, and moved funds between branches by written order — a giro system centuries before its European reinvention.
nodes.src: Sitta von Reden, Money in Ptolemaic Egypt (2007); Catharine Lorber, Coins of the Ptolemaic Empire (2018– ). Banking: Raymond Bogaert, Banques et banquiers dans les cités grecques (1968) and his Egyptian studies.

nodes.label: The temples in the Ptolemaic economy
nodes.full: The temples were huge economic actors — land, herds, workshops, dependent labour — and the Ptolemies both funded and squeezed them. Ptolemy II converted the old temple harvest-tax, the apomoira, into revenue for the cult of the deified Arsinoe, and replaced some temple income with a fixed state subsidy, the syntaxis, tightening royal control. The wealth the southern temples still commanded is part of what bankrolled the twenty-year secession of the Thebaid.
nodes.src: Apomoira and syntaxis: Willy Clarysse & Katelijn Vandorpe, and P.Rev. cols.24–37. J.G. Manning, Land and Power in Ptolemaic Egypt (2003). Temple wealth and the revolt: Veïsse, Les 'révoltes égyptiennes' (2004).

nodes.label: The Red Sea ports and the eastern trade
nodes.full: The Ptolemies opened Egypt's Red Sea coast. Ptolemy II founded the ports of Myos Hormos and Berenike and cut a caravan road to them from Coptos on the Nile, at first to land war elephants captured in Africa, then increasingly for incense, ivory, gold, tortoiseshell and — by the end of the period — goods from India. It was the infrastructure on which the far larger Roman-era Indian Ocean trade would be built.
nodes.src: Steven Sidebotham, Berenike and the Ancient Maritime Spice Route (2011); the Berenike excavation reports (Sidebotham & Wendrich). The Coptos–Berenike road: the Paneion inscriptions; the 'Pithom Stela' on the elephant trade.

nodes.label: The Pharos of Alexandria
nodes.full: The lighthouse built for Ptolemy I and II by Sostratus of Cnidus on the island of Pharos rose in three diminishing stages — a square base, an octagonal middle, a round top — to somewhere over a hundred metres, with a fire (and, later accounts say, a mirror) at the summit whose light was visible far out to sea. It was counted among the Seven Wonders, gave every European language its word for 'lighthouse', and stood, damaged by earthquakes, until the fourteenth century AD.
nodes.src: Strabo 17.1.6; Pliny 36.83; the poem of Posidippus. Hermann Thiersch, Pharos: Antike, Islam und Occident (1909); Jean-Yves Empereur, Le Phare d'Alexandrie (1998), incorporating the underwater blocks recovered from 1994.

nodes.label: Alexandrian mechanics and pneumatics
nodes.full: Alexandria became the centre of Greek applied mechanics. Ktesibios built the force pump, an accurate water clock, the water-organ and an air-spring catapult; Philo of Byzantium wrote a multi-volume Mechanike Syntaxis covering artillery, pneumatics, siegecraft and automata; and the tradition continued to Hero in the Roman period. Much of it was showpiece engineering — temple doors that opened by fire, self-filling wine bowls — but the underlying grasp of air pressure, siphons and gearing was real.
nodes.src: Philo of Byzantium, Pneumatica and Belopoeica. A.G. Drachmann, Ktesibios, Philon and Heron (1948) and The Mechanical Technology of Greek and Roman Antiquity (1963); Serafina Cuomo, Technology and Culture in Greek and Roman Antiquity (2007).

nodes.label: The waterwheel and the screw
nodes.full: Two water-lifting devices spread through Ptolemaic Egypt and stayed for two thousand years. The saqiya — a vertical wheel carrying a chain of pots, turned by an ox through a right-angle gear — could raise water several metres for perennial irrigation. The 'Archimedean' screw, a helix in a cylinder cranked by hand or foot, lifted water for gardens, mine drainage and the reclaimed Faiyum. Together they let land be cropped year-round instead of only on the flood.
nodes.src: Thorkild Schiøler, Roman and Islamic Water-Lifting Wheels (1973); John Peter Oleson, Greek and Roman Mechanical Water-Lifting Devices (1984). The screw: Diodorus 1.34, 5.37; Vitruvius 10.6.

nodes.label: War elephants and giant ships
nodes.full: The Successor kingdoms ran a military technology race, and the Ptolemies competed. Lacking access to Indian elephants, they mounted hunting expeditions down the African coast for the smaller forest elephant, shipped the animals north in special transports, and kept elephant stables at Alexandria — 73 of them fought at Raphia. The dynasty also built the era's largest warships, culminating in Ptolemy IV's 'forty', a showpiece catamaran said to need 4,000 rowers, more spectacle than weapon.
nodes.src: Elephants: the Pithom Stela; Polybius 5.84 on Raphia; H.H. Scullard, The Elephant in the Greek and Roman World (1974). The 'forty': Athenaeus 5.203e–204d; Lionel Casson, Ships and Seamanship (1971) pp.108–12.

nodes.label: Building the last Egyptian temples
nodes.full: The Ptolemaic temple-builders worked to a repeated master plan and a long timescale. Sandstone was quarried at Gebel el-Silsila and floated downstream; a mud-brick enclosure went up first; the stone temple rose within it course by course, decorated as it went, its walls honeycombed with hidden crypts for the cult treasure. Edfu took 180 years and six kings from foundation to finished gate — and, being finished, is the one Egyptian temple that still stands essentially complete.
nodes.src: Dieter Arnold, Building in Egypt: Pharaonic Stone Masonry (1991) and Temples of the Last Pharaohs (1999). Edfu building history: the temple's dedicatory texts, Chassinat, Le temple d'Edfou VII (1932).

nodes.label: The Indian Ocean route opens
nodes.full: Late in the period Greek sailors based in Egypt worked out how to use the monsoon to cross the open ocean to India and back, instead of coasting. Poseidonius and Strabo tell of Eudoxus of Cyzicus, sent by Ptolemy VIII, making the voyage twice with an Indian castaway as guide; the pilot Hippalus is later credited with the monsoon route. Direct Egypt–India sailing was still a trickle, but it laid the foundation for the Roman-era trade that sent a hundred ships a year.
nodes.src: Strabo 2.3.4–5 (Eudoxus, from Poseidonius); Periplus Maris Erythraei 57 (Hippalus). Lionel Casson, The Periplus Maris Erythraei (1989); Raoul McLaughlin, The Roman Empire and the Indian Ocean (2014).

nodes.label: Egypt in the Hellenistic system
nodes.full: For its first century the Ptolemaic kingdom was a Mediterranean great power: garrisons and protectorates from Cyrene through Cyprus and Coele-Syria to the coasts of Anatolia and Thrace, leadership of a league of Aegean islands, and a fleet to match the Antigonids'. It exported more than soldiers — the cult of Isis and Serapis, the poetry and scholarship of Alexandria, and a style of divine monarchy that the other Hellenistic courts imitated.
nodes.src: Hölbl, A History of the Ptolemaic Empire (2001) pp.36–58; Roger Bagnall, The Administration of the Ptolemaic Possessions outside Egypt (1976). The island league: the Nesiotic League inscriptions.

nodes.label: The Septuagint and Jewish-Greek culture
nodes.full: At Alexandria the Hebrew Torah was translated into Greek — the Septuagint — a project the later Letter of Aristeas dressed up as seventy-two elders working in isolation at royal request. Whatever its real origin, it made the Jewish scriptures readable to a Greek-speaking world and to Greek-speaking Jews who no longer knew Hebrew, and it seeded a Jewish-Greek literature (Ezekiel the Tragedian's drama on the Exodus, 3 Maccabees) that culminated, under Rome, in Philo.
nodes.src: Letter of Aristeas; Sylvie Honigman, The Septuagint and Homeric Scholarship in Alexandria (2003); Tessa Rajak, Translation and Survival (2009). Corpus Papyrorum Judaicarum (1957–64).

nodes.label: Meroe and the shared frontier
nodes.full: South of the First Cataract, Ptolemaic Egypt met the kingdom of Meroe. The border strip, the 'Twelve-Mile Land' or Dodekaschoinos, was jointly exploited and dotted with temples both sides supported; Philae drew Nubian pilgrims and its priests corresponded with Meroe. Contact ran from trade in gold, ivory, ebony and animals through Meroïtic embassies to occasional raiding, but for most of the period the two Nile states managed a working coexistence.
nodes.src: László Török, Between Two Worlds: The Frontier Region between Ancient Nubia and Egypt (2009); Stanley Burstein, 'The Ptolemaic Kings and the Kingdom of Meroe', in Graeco-Africana (1995).

nodes.label: Egypt drawn into Rome's orbit
nodes.full: From a treaty of friendship in 273 BC, Rome's involvement deepened into control. Ptolemies travelled to the Senate to plead for backing; Roman envoys settled dynastic disputes; a Roman army restored Ptolemy XII in 55 and left the 'Gabiniani' garrison; Egypt's revenues were mortgaged to Roman financiers. Rome wanted the grain and the treasury and feared letting any one Roman have them — which is why annexation waited until Octavian could take Egypt as his private domain.
nodes.src: Livy, Periochae; Cicero; Dio 39. Erich Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984); Günther Hölbl (2001) pp.181–230.

nodes.label: Greeks and Egyptians blend in the chora
nodes.full: In the countryside the two populations slowly merged. Mixed marriages became common; people carried a Greek and an Egyptian name and used whichever suited the document; Egyptians entered the Greek-speaking administration and, after Raphia, the phalanx; Greek soldier-families adopted Egyptian gods and Egyptian burial. By the end of the period the chora held a Greco-Egyptian population that was not quite either — the society Rome would inherit and tax by ethnic category.
nodes.src: Willy Clarysse, 'Greeks and Egyptians in the Ptolemaic Army and Administration', Aegyptus 65 (1985); Dorothy Thompson & Willy Clarysse, Counting the People in Hellenistic Egypt (2006); Jane Rowlandson (ed.), Women and Society in Greek and Roman Egypt (1998).

nodes.label: Alexandria the cosmopolis
nodes.full: Within a century of its founding Alexandria was the largest city in the Greek-speaking world, with a population plausibly over 300,000: Greeks and Macedonians, native Egyptians, one of the biggest Jewish communities anywhere, Syrians, Anatolians, Nubians, and sailors from everywhere. It had a grid of paved streets, running water, twin harbours, a famously volatile crowd that made and unmade kings, and the wealth of a continent passing through it — the first true multiethnic megacity.
nodes.src: Strabo 17.1.6–13; Polybius 34.14 (the three populations). P.M. Fraser, Ptolemaic Alexandria (1972); Diana Delia, 'The Population of Roman Alexandria', TAPA 118 (1988) for the numbers debate.

nodes.label: The Nile and the desert roads
nodes.full: Ptolemaic Egypt faced three ways from one river. The Nile flood still set the year and the tax assessment; the re-cut canal linked it to the Red Sea; new guarded roads with wells crossed the Eastern Desert from Coptos to the ports of Myos Hormos and Berenike; and the Western oases — Kharga, Dakhla, Bahariya — were tied in by their own temples and garrisons. The desert was no longer just a wall but a set of managed corridors to Africa, Arabia and, eventually, India.
nodes.src: Steven Sidebotham, Berenike and the Ancient Maritime Spice Route (2011); the Coptos tariff and the Eastern Desert praesidia. Oasis integration: Olaf Kaper on Dakhla; the 'Ayn Manawir archive.

nodes.label: Meroe at its height
nodes.full: South of the Ptolemaic frontier the kingdom of Meroe reached its peak: royal pyramids at Meroe and the earlier sites, temples to Amun and to the lion-god Apedemak, a large-scale iron industry whose slag heaps still ring the capital, and, from about 180 BC, its own alphabetic script for the Meroïtic language, replacing Egyptian in official use. Ruled often by powerful queens, the kandakes, it was a fully independent African civilisation trading and negotiating with Egypt as an equal.
nodes.src: Derek Welsby, The Kingdom of Kush: The Napatan and Meroitic Empires (1996); László Török, The Kingdom of Kush (1997). Meroïtic script: Claude Rilly, La langue du royaume de Méroé (2007). The iron industry: recent UCL work reassessing the 'Birmingham of Africa' claim.

nodes.label: Volcanoes, low Niles and revolt
nodes.full: For all the state's management, the country lived at the mercy of the flood. Recent work matching ice-core records of large volcanic eruptions to Nile gauge data and papyrus evidence finds that eruption years suppressed the summer monsoon over the Ethiopian highlands, weakened the flood, and were repeatedly followed by hardship and unrest — including at the outbreak of the Great Revolt of the Thebaid and in later crises. The Ptolemaic economy's weak point was the sky over East Africa.
nodes.src: Joseph Manning, Francis Ludlow et al., 'Volcanic suppression of Nile summer flooding triggers revolt and constrains interstate conflict in ancient Egypt', Nature Communications 8 (2017).

nodes.label: Cleopatra VII, the last pharaoh
nodes.full: Cleopatra was the first Ptolemy in three centuries to learn Egyptian, and Plutarch says she could deal with envoys from nine nations in their own tongue. She was a working monarch — restoring finances, managing the priesthoods, presenting herself as the goddess Isis and as pharaoh in temple relief — who staked the kingdom's survival on partnership with the two most powerful Romans of her age. The victors wrote her up as a seductress and Rome's enemy; the documents show an able ruler out of options.
nodes.src: Plutarch, Antony 27, 29. Duane Roller, Cleopatra: A Biography (2010); Joyce Tyldesley, Cleopatra: Last Queen of Egypt (2008); Prudence Jones, Cleopatra: A Sourcebook (2006).

nodes.label: Arsinoe II, the deified queen
nodes.full: Arsinoe II lived three royal lives: married at sixteen to the aged Lysimachus of Thrace, then to her murderous half-brother Ptolemy Keraunos, then — back in Egypt — to her full brother Ptolemy II, with whom she was worshipped as one of the 'Sibling Gods'. Whether she governed or merely symbolised, her name is everywhere: a Faiyum nome, a Red Sea port, a festival, a priestess in her own cult, and a share of the offerings in every temple in Egypt after her death.
nodes.src: Elizabeth Carney, Arsinoë of Egypt and Macedon: A Royal Life (2013). The Mendes Stela and the Pithom Stela on her cult; the Grand Procession featured her.

nodes.label: The scholars of the Museum
nodes.full: The Museum's members were court intellectuals living on royal patronage: Zenodotus and then Aristophanes of Byzantium and Aristarchus building the critical text of Homer; Callimachus compiling the 120-book catalogue of the Library while feuding in verse with Apollonius of Rhodes; Eratosthenes running the place while measuring the Earth. A hostile epigram called them 'well-fed bookworms squabbling endlessly in the Muses' birdcage' — but they invented the disciplines of textual criticism and scholarship.
nodes.src: The 'birdcage of the Muses': Timon of Phlius via Athenaeus 1.22d. Rudolf Pfeiffer, History of Classical Scholarship (1968); P.M. Fraser, Ptolemaic Alexandria (1972) vol.1 pp.447–79.

nodes.label: Zenon, the estate manager
nodes.full: Zenon of Caunus came to Egypt as the business agent of the finance minister Apollonios and stayed to run his model estate at Philadelphia. His archive — over 1,700 papyri, kept because he hoarded everything — is the fullest window into any single life from the ancient world: crop accounts, building contracts, lawsuits, a pet-animal shipment, and letters from Egyptian workers on the estate protesting that they are cheated of pay 'because I am not a Greek'.
nodes.src: Zenon archive: P.Cair.Zen. I–V (Edgar), P.Lond. VII, P.Mich. I. Pieter Pestman, A Guide to the Zenon Archive (1981); the complaint of the camel-herd Senchons and of a workman 'because I do not know how to Hellenize'.

nodes.label: The choachytes of Thebes
nodes.full: On the Theban west bank a guild of Egyptian mortuary priests, the choachytes or 'water-pourers', maintained the tombs and mummies of paying clients, performed the offerings, and traded the rights to particular burials among themselves like property. Their family archives, in Demotic and Greek, run for generations and show a self-governing native middle class — with its own association, arbitration rules and mixed-language contracts — carrying on an Egyptian profession under a Greek state.
nodes.src: The Theban choachyte archives (e.g. the archive of Amenothes son of Horos; P. Survey / the 'archive of the Theban choachytes'): Pieter Pestman, L'archivio di Amenothes figlio di Horos (1981) and The Archive of the Theban Choachytes (1993).

nodes.label: Ptolemaios, the recluse of the Serapeum
nodes.full: Ptolemaios son of Glaukias, of Macedonian descent, spent more than twenty years shut up 'in confinement' (katoche) inside the temple of Serapis at Memphis, unable or unwilling to leave. His archive of about a hundred documents preserves his petitions about being assaulted and cheated, his careful records of his own dreams, and his sponsorship of two Egyptian twin girls, Thaues and Taous, who served the god — a strange, intimate case study of temple dependency and a life lived between Greek and Egyptian identities.
nodes.src: UPZ I (Wilcken, 1927); the 'Serapeum archive'. Dorothy Thompson, Memphis under the Ptolemies (1988, 2nd ed. 2012) pp.212–65; Sandra Coussement and others on the twins and the katoche.

nodes.label: Manetho, Petosiris and the priest between two worlds
nodes.full: A class of Egyptian priest-scholars translated their own tradition for the new rulers and for a Greek audience. Manetho of Sebennytos wrote Egypt's dynastic history in Greek; the high priest Petosiris at Hermopolis built a tomb-chapel whose reliefs put Egyptian ritual scenes into Greek-influenced style and drapery, its texts urging the reader toward the 'path of god'; and an astrological literature circulated under the names of the sage Petosiris and a legendary king Nechepso. These men held the two cultures in one head.
nodes.src: Tomb of Petosiris: Gustave Lefebvre, Le tombeau de Petosiris (1923–24). Manetho: Waddell's Loeb (1940). The Nechepso–Petosiris astrological corpus: Ernst Riess's fragments; Kim Ryholt on the tradition.
